52-year-old man with sudden dyspnea. CT pulmonary angiography for suspected pulmonary embolism (1 mm slices). Other clinical data not available.
Referta l'angio-TC: arterie polmonari, p: Report the CT angiography: pulmonary arteries, then parenchyma and heart, then the conclusion and what you do.
Lettura dell'angio-TC polmonare: si segu:
Reading CT pulmonary angiography: each artery is followed from the trunk to the segmental branches and, if quality allows, to the subsegmental ones, with a wide window (for example 100/700) so as not to "burn out" the thrombi in the contrast. An acute embolus is a central filling defect surrounded by contrast ("polo mint" sign in cross-section, "railway track" sign in longitudinal section) or an occlusion with a vessel of normal or increased caliber; chronic embolism instead has eccentric thrombi adherent to the wall, bands and webs, narrowed vessels.

After the thrombi, always look at the right heart, because it determines severity: ratio of the right to left ventricular diameter (> 1 unfavorable), straightened interventricular septum or bowed toward the left, reflux of contrast into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins (present in this case, with an RV/LV ratio on axial images of about 1.5 or more). Then the parenchyma: infarcts (peripheral pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacities), effusion, alternative diagnoses.

Acute pulmonary embolism is a critical finding to be communicated immediately, by voice, to the physician caring for the patient, and to be recorded in the report (to whom, when, how). Risk stratification (sPESI, echocardiogram, troponin) and treatment (anticoagulation; thrombolysis only if hemodynamically unstable) are up to the clinician, but the radiologist must write the signs of right heart strain.
